  trauma_type: Police

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Threat: Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory

Vignette:
Malik Washington was a forty-six-year-old curriculum designer when a routine drive home from a late meeting split his life into a before and an after. A taillight was out, something he had simply not noticed, and when the police cruiser’s lights flared in his mirror he pulled over immediately, turning off the engine, his hands on the wheel exactly as he believed he was supposed to do. What followed happened very fast and yet felt interminable: the shouting, the door wrenched open, his body dragged across the asphalt, his wrists locked behind him. He kept asking what he had done but the questions were lost in the noise. He was processed, held for hours, and released without charges, but the arbitrariness of it all—the sheer speed with which his agency had been stripped away—lodged itself deep inside him.

The event itself became a paradox he could not solve. He was entirely unable to put it into words. When his wife, Nia, asked what had happened, the story collapsed before it reached his lips, dissolving into a thick, wordless pressure in his chest. Sometimes that pressure arrived on its own, in the middle of the day, carrying the full emotional intensity of the terror without any clear image attached—just the sickening plunge, the hot shame, the racing heart. At other times a specific trigger would drop him directly into a memory, and it would hit him so powerfully that he had to stop whatever he was doing. He would sit frozen at his desk or excuse himself mid-sentence from a meeting, locking himself in a bathroom stall until the wave passed.

In his office, the world began to feel permanently dangerous. He found himself scanning every parking lot before walking to his car, cataloguing exits, noting the position of every patrol car he passed. A colleague touching his shoulder to get his attention made him jump violently, his body reacting before his mind could catch up. As a curriculum designer, his work had once involved regular field testing in schools across the district, but those routes took him past the precinct where he had been held, and every time he approached that intersection his heart hammered so hard in his chest that he felt he could not think straight. He quietly volunteered for remote desk projects, telling his supervisor he preferred the focus of solitary work. The truth was simpler: he could not bear the physical cost of the commute. He began taking a forty-minute detour that drained him, but the alternative—that sickening physical flood of recognition—felt unmanageable.

He had come to believe that he was fundamentally changed, cracked in a way that could not be repaired. His own jumpiness felt like evidence of weakness, a character flaw he could not overcome. He was constantly on guard, and that vigilance exhausted him. At home, Nia felt the distance growing. She wanted to understand, but he could not give her the story. She wanted to go to dinner downtown, but the idea of driving at night, of the dark and the tail lights, left him paralyzed with an unnamed dread. He grew irritable, snapping at minor surprises, and then hating himself for it.

The moment that finally brought him to the clinic came during a routine team meeting to review a new unit on community safety. He felt it hit him first as pure, unbidden emotion—terror, humiliation, helplessness—without any image to anchor it. His throat closed, his hands trembled, and he had to leave the room. In the parking lot he nearly vomited. He sat in his car staring at the steering wheel, realizing he could no longer outrun a reaction that was living inside him full-time, waiting to emerge. He drove straight to the clinic.

He is terrified of what therapy will ask of him—of having to narrate a story he cannot put into words, of being overwhelmed by the very memories he has spent almost two years avoiding. What frightened him most was the unpredictability of his own body, the sense that safety could be ripped away at any moment. He hopes, quietly, for a way to stop living in a state of constant, wordless alarm. He hopes to feel like himself again.
